WASDI application
Landslide Detection (Sentinel-1)
Spotting landslides from space

From radar physics and statistics to the two apps that turn a Sentinel-1 pass into a map of landslides: explained step by step, with interactive demos, and tested on two real disasters.

Overview

Find the slopes that moved, even under cloud

After a hurricane or an earthquake, hillsides fail, roads are cut and villages can be buried. Emergency teams need to know where, fast. The trouble is that the same storm that triggers landslides also fills the sky with cloud, so ordinary satellite photos are often useless. Radar is not.

The Sentinel-1 satellites send their own radio pulses down to the ground and record what bounces back. This works at night and through cloud and rain. When a slope slides, the surface and the vegetation on it change, and so does the echo. The WASDI Landslide Detection app looks for exactly that change, and this page explains, from first principles, how it does it.

Day and nightradar needs no sunlight
Through cloudstorms do not block it

1You choose where and whenDraw a box on the map and give the date of the storm or earthquake.

3It flags likely landslidesChanges on steep ground that look like a slide are mapped. Everything else is ignored.

WHYWhy detect landslides from space?

Landslides are among the deadliest secondary hazards of heavy rain, hurricanes and earthquakes. They often strike steep, remote terrain that is slow and dangerous to survey on foot right after the triggering event. Three facts shape the whole design of this app.

01 · Timing

They cluster exactly when conditions are worst

Most landslides are triggered by heavy, prolonged rain that saturates hillside soil until it fails under its own weight. The days right after a major storm are both the most likely time for new slides and the hardest time to reach them.

02 · Visibility

Optical satellites go blind at the worst moment

The storm that triggers the slides also blankets the region in thick cloud for days. A camera-like (optical) satellite cannot see through cloud, precisely when responders most need fresh imagery.

03 · Radar

Radar brings its own light and sees through cloud

Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites carry their own source of illumination and see through cloud, smoke and darkness. Sentinel-1 revisits the same ground every few days, whatever the weather.

The aim, concretely. Given one or more Sentinel-1 passes from before and after a suspected event, over an area of interest, automatically produce a map of exactly which pixels show the radar signature of a fresh landslide, without waiting for cloud-free optical imagery and without a person comparing before/after images by eye.

APPSTwo apps that work as a team

What you run in WASDI is usually the automatic app. It does the searching for you: you give it an area and a date, it finds the right Sentinel-1 images. Behind it sits the manual app, which contains all of the detection mathematics and works on one list of satellite tracks that it is handed.

They are not two algorithms. They are two doors into the same one. If you already know exactly which radar scenes you want to compare, you can call the manual app directly. If a storm has just hit and nobody has chosen orbit numbers and filenames, the automatic app finds them for you.

A satellite track (an "orbit", or more exactly a relative orbit) is one repeating path over the Earth. Looking at the same place from two different tracks gives two different views of the same slope. The next tabs show why that helps.

The full step-by-step chain of both apps, as a flow chart, is on the Pipeline tab.

Key terms at a glance

TermIn plain words
BackscatterThe share of the radar pulse that bounces back to the satellite. Its strength depends on how rough, wet and steep the surface is.
SpeckleThe grainy, salt-and-pepper texture present in every radar image, caused by waves interfering with each other. It is removed before any comparison.
Decibel (dB)A logarithmic scale, so that a doubling always looks like the same step. Backscatter changes are compared in dB.
BaselineThe "normal" for each pixel, built from several radar images taken before the event: a typical value and how much it naturally wobbles.
Z-scoreHow many "typical wobbles" the post-event value sits away from that pixel's own normal.
Polarization (VH, VV)Sentinel-1 records two kinds of echo at once. A real change tends to show in both; noise rarely does.
Percentile thresholdA cut-off set from the scene's own scores (for example the top 0.5%), so it adapts to calm and stormy scenes alike.
HysteresisA two-level test: a weak condition to be considered, a strong condition (somewhere in the same region) to be accepted.
DEMDigital Elevation Model, a terrain height map. It gives the slope of every pixel.
Orbit / trackOne repeating satellite path. Different tracks view the same slope from different directions.
Radar physics

What radar measures, and why a landslide changes it

A camera records sunlight reflected by the surface. A radar sends its own microwave pulse and records how much of it comes back. That returned energy is called backscatter, and it depends heavily on how rough or smooth the surface is.

In this section

1.1Backscatter: the echo from the ground

The middle slope is covered by forest. Its leaves and branches scatter plenty of the pulse back to the satellite, so it appears bright in a radar image.

Think of throwing a ball at a wall. Against a rough, uneven wall it bounces back in many directions and some of it returns to you. Against a smooth, tilted mirror it ricochets away. A radar pulse behaves the same way. The symbol for backscatter is σ0: the fraction of the transmitted pulse that a surface sends back per unit area, calibrated so that images from different dates can be compared.

Backscatter depends on three things above all: the roughness of the surface compared with the radar wavelength, its moisture (wet ground reflects more), and its slope relative to the beam. Sentinel-1 operates in the C-band, a wavelength of about 5.6 cm, so leaves, twigs, soil clods and stones are all the right size to scatter it.

Calm water behaves like a mirror: it reflects the pulse away from the satellite, so it appears almost black. Forest is a jumble of scatterers: it appears bright.

1.2Why a landslide changes the echo

A landslide strips vegetation and soil from the source area (the steep upper section where the slide starts) and leaves behind smoother bare ground or rock. That smoother surface reflects the pulse more like a mirror, mostly away from the satellite. The result is a drop in backscatter at the same location between a "before" and an "after" pass. That drop is the core signal this app looks for.

It happens within seconds, whereas natural changes (crops growing, soil drying, seasons) happen slowly and tend to change the echo gently. A sudden, strong, localized drop on steep ground is unusual, and that is what the statistics on the next tab quantify.

An important, specific detail. General landslide literature often mentions backscatter increasing in the rough debris pile at the bottom of a slope. This app deliberately targets the source area or scarp instead, where the typical response is a backscatter decrease. That is why the terrain filter is called a source slope filter, and why every threshold in the app is built to detect drops, not rises.

1.3Radar looks sideways

A camera on a satellite looks straight down. A radar like Sentinel-1 looks obliquely, to the side, because it measures distance by timing the echo. That has three consequences on steep terrain, all of which matter for landslides:

Foreshortening

Slopes facing the satellite are squashed

A slope tilted toward the beam occupies fewer pixels than it should and is compressed in the image, with a strong, bright return.

Layover

Steep faces can fold over

On very steep slopes facing the satellite, the top can be recorded before the bottom, so the image folds over itself and the information is mixed up.

Shadow

Slopes facing away can be hidden

A slope tilted away from the beam, steeper than the beam angle, is never illuminated at all. No echo means nothing can be detected there from that direction.

The same hillside therefore looks different from different satellite tracks. A slope that is hidden in shadow from one track is clearly visible from another. This is the reason the app can combine several tracks (see multi-orbit fusion) and why a single track can miss a slide that its neighbour sees.

1.4Speckle: why every radar image is grainy

Even over a perfectly uniform field or calm lake, a raw radar image looks grainy. This salt-and-pepper texture is called speckle. It is not ordinary sensor noise. It comes from how radar imaging works.

Each ground resolution cell contains many small scatterers (blades of grass, soil grains, rock facets). Each reflects the radar wave back over a slightly different path length. At the sensor, the many small echoes add up wave by wave: sometimes reinforcing, sometimes cancelling out. A patch of ground whose physical properties are perfectly uniform can therefore still produce wildly different brightness values from one pixel to the next.

Speckle is multiplicative: it scales with the signal rather than adding a fixed amount, and it is spatially random. Comparing two dates pixel by pixel is unreliable until it is suppressed, because a speckle spike can look just like a change.

Speckle lab

The panels below simulate a hillside with one sharp-edged dark patch (a stand-in for a scarp) on uniform ground. Panel two is what the radar actually delivers. Try the two common smoothing filters and the window size. Watch two numbers: how much the noise in the flat area is reduced, and how much the filter widens a sharp edge. A good filter reduces the first without widening the second.

Filter
-noise in flat area, raw (dB)
-noise after filter (dB)
-edge blur added by the filter (pixels)

The median replaces each pixel by the middle value of its neighbours, so isolated bright or dark spikes are discarded, and a straight edge is never blurred by the filter itself (the middle value is always one of the two levels). The plain average smooths a little more, but smears every edge. The edge number is measured on the noise-free scene, so it shows only the blur the filter itself adds. In very grainy images, noise can still make a filtered edge ragged, which is why the window is kept small.

1.5Pre-processing: from raw scene to analysis-ready image

Before any statistics, every Sentinel-1 scene goes through the same fixed recipe. Both apps use it, so a pre-event scene and a post-event scene are always treated identically. The calibration and despeckling are run through an ESA SNAP workflow, and the order of the steps matters.

  1. CalibrateConvert the raw digital numbers of the GRD (ground range detected) product into physical backscatter, so that dates are comparable.
  2. Dual-polKeep both channels, VH and VV, as linear backscatter. They respond differently to the surface (explained on the Statistics tab).
  3. Fill gapsGaps with no data (scene edges, shadow) are filled from the nearest valid neighbour before filtering.
  4. DespeckleA 5×5 median filter is applied in the linear power domain, before conversion to decibels.
  5. To decibelsConvert to dB so that a doubling is the same step everywhere. Only now does the image feed the statistics.

Why the order matters

  • Filtering across a raw edge into a patch of zero-valued no-data would drag a false dark halo into the result, so gaps are filled first.
  • Speckle is multiplicative and defined on the power scale. Filtering values that are already logarithmic would distort the result, so despeckling is done before the dB conversion.

Why a median, not an average

  • The median knocks down speckle's random spikes while a real sharp edge, like a scarp boundary, is not blurred by the filter itself, which an average always does (see the lab above).
  • It is robust: one extreme pixel in a window of 25 cannot move the result.
The statistics

Turning "backscatter dropped" into one reliable number per pixel

Radar images are naturally noisy. Even two images of the exact same untouched hillside, taken days apart, differ pixel by pixel. A method that just compared one "before" image with one "after" image would be swamped by that variation. So the app first builds a small statistical model of normal for every pixel, and only then asks how unusual the post-event image is.

In this section

2.1The simplest idea: a log ratio

The classic building block of radar change detection is to divide the post-event backscatter by the pre-event backscatter and express the result in decibels:

Backscatter change in decibels RatiodB = 10 · log10σ0preσ0post

Decibels squeeze the huge natural range of radar brightness into a scale where a doubling is always the same step, whatever the starting brightness. It is the same reason sound loudness is quoted in decibels rather than raw pressure. As a rule of thumb, 3 dB is a factor of two and 10 dB is a factor of ten.

On its own, a single before/after pair is too noisy to trust: speckle and ordinary day-to-day variation add their own random ups and downs. So the app does not stop here.

See the change first

A simulated mountain scene with five hidden landslides. Drag the handle and look for where the echo went dark between the two images. Some dark patches are real slides. Some are not.

BeforeAfterSimulated

2.2A real baseline, not just one photo

Instead of one pre-event image, the app collects several from the same satellite track: 2 at minimum, 3 to 4 or more recommended, and 4 by default. For every pixel it computes two numbers from those images:

  • the median: a stable "typical" value, resistant to any single noisy image;
  • the standard deviation (the spread): how much that particular pixel normally wobbles from one image to the next.

The second number is what makes the method fair. A pixel on a calm, steady surface wobbles very little, so a small change there is remarkable. A pixel on a restless, windblown or wet surface wobbles a lot, so the same change means little. The post-event value is then judged against the pixel's own habits, not against a single global rule.

The pre-event images are chosen from the 100 days before the event by default. Taking them from the same relative orbit means the satellite looks at the ground at the same angle each time, so differences are not caused by changing viewing geometry.

2.3The Z-score: how unusual is the post-event value?

Combine the two ideas and you get one number per pixel and per polarization:

The Z-score Z = σ0post,dB − median(σ0pre,dB)max( std(σ0pre,dB) , SIGMA_FLOOR_DB )

Put in plain words: Z counts how many "typical wobbles" the post-event value sits away from this pixel's own normal range. It is not an absolute decibel change, but a change sized relative to how much that specific pixel naturally jumps around. A Z of −1 is unremarkable background noise almost everywhere. A Z of −6 is not, whatever the raw decibel numbers behind it.

TermWhat it actually is
σ0Radar jargon for backscatter: the fraction of the transmitted pulse a surface sends back per unit area. The superscript "0" marks it as the normalized, calibrated quantity rather than a raw sensor count.
σ0post,dBThis exact pixel's backscatter in the post-event image, in decibels, after despeckling. One number, for one polarization, at one location.
median(σ0pre,dB)This same pixel's typical backscatter across every pre-event image supplied for this orbit. The baseline from 2.2, computed once per pixel.
std(σ0pre,dB)This same pixel's own natural spread across those pre-event images: how noisy or stable that specific spot normally is, not a scene-wide average.
SIGMA_FLOOR_DBA configured minimum for the denominator, 0.35 dB by default. Without it, a pixel that happened to look identical in every pre-event image would have a near-zero spread, and dividing by that would turn an ordinary, tiny change into an artificially huge Z.

Try the Z-score

Four pre-event measurements (dark dots) set the typical value and the spread. Drag the sliders to change how much the pixel normally wobbles and how far backscatter drops after the event.

Try a very steady pixel (wobble near 0.05) with the floor off: a tiny 1 dB drop produces a huge Z. Switch the floor on and it is held back to a sensible value.

2.4More than one post-event image? The aggregation options

A track can be given several post-event images, for instance to bridge a gap in the archive or to keep watching a slope for days after the event. The setting POST_AGGREGATION decides how those several decibel differences, at the same pixel, collapse into the single number the Z-score uses. It is applied before the Z-score formula: the result becomes the post-event value in that formula, per polarization, per pixel.

ModeHow it is computedWhat it trades off
closest (default)Only the single post-event image closest to the event is used. Any others supplied are logged and ignored.Simple and predictable, and matches the original single-image behaviour exactly, but it throws away any extra post-event images.
medianThe per-pixel median of the difference across every supplied post-event image.Extra speckle suppression by averaging over more looks, at the cost of blurring a real signal that fades or partly recovers between acquisitions (debris settling, vegetation regrowing).
max_anomalyPer pixel, whichever supplied image shows the single strongest (most negative) backscatter drop.Maximizes recall for a signal that fades or recovers quickly, but is more exposed to a one-off noisy dip in a single image being mistaken for a sustained change.

One pixel, four post-event images

The bars show the backscatter drop seen at one pixel in four acquisitions after a slide. The signal is strongest on the second pass and then recovers. Choose a mode to see which value the Z-score would receive.

In the Jamaica tests, max_anomaly recovered a real, partial detection at a site that closest had missed entirely, while median reshaped detections at the other sites without turning them into noise. Details are on the Real events tab.

2.5Using both polarizations: dual-pol fusion

Polarization is the orientation in which the radar wave oscillates. Sentinel-1 transmits in one orientation and records the echo in two: VV (received in the same orientation, dominated by scattering from the surface itself) and VH (received in the crossed orientation, which is strongly influenced by vegetation and rough, volume-like scattering). They respond differently to the same ground, so a real change tends to show in both, while a random noise spike rarely does.

The app computes a Z-score for each polarization, keeps only the negative deviations (drops, the signature from Tab 2), and combines them into one score D. It works in two steps.

Step A: keep only dropsZ− = min( Z , 0 )
Step B: combine like a vector lengthD = √( (Z−VH)2 + (Z−VV)2 )

Step A. If backscatter went up at a pixel (Z positive), Z− is forced to exactly 0, so that polarization contributes nothing. Only real drops survive, in each polarization separately. Step B. This is the same arithmetic as the length of the hypotenuse of a right triangle: square both, add, take the root. Treating the two scores as perpendicular axes of one small vector has a useful effect: a strong drop in either polarization alone still gives a sizeable D, while a drop present in both at once gives a larger D than either alone, without one channel being averaged away by the other.

ZVHZVVZ−VHZ−VVDReading
−4.0+0.5−4.004.00Drop in one polarization only: still flagged
−3.0−3.0−3.0−3.04.24A smaller drop in both scores higher than the larger one in one channel
+2.0+1.0000.00Backscatter rose: no evidence of a landslide here

Why not simply add the two? A plain sum would let one enormous drop in a single polarization (possibly a processing artefact) dominate the total exactly as a genuine two-channel detection would, and it would pass any noise in the second channel straight through. The squared-and-rooted form makes single-channel and dual-channel evidence combine in a way that rewards agreement between the channels instead of just tallying them.

Explore the fusion

Where this leaves us. Every pixel now carries a single anomaly score D: zero where nothing dropped, and larger the more surprising and the more polarization-consistent the drop. The next tab turns that score map into a clean map of landslides.

Refining the detection

From a noisy anomaly score to a clean, plausible map

The fused score D still needs several more ideas before it becomes a trustworthy landslide mask: where to draw the line, how to keep fuzzy true edges but not noise, whether the terrain even makes physical sense, how to tidy the shapes, and what to do when more than one satellite track is available.

  1. ThresholdCore and extent cut-offs from the scene's own percentiles.
  2. LinkHysteresis keeps extent regions that touch a core pixel.
  3. TidySlope gate, closing, size and shape filters, cluster mode.
  4. FuseCombine satellite tracks: either, both, or a support count.
In this section

3.1Adaptive thresholds: let the scene set the bar

First, the score map is gently smoothed with a moving window (SCORE_SMOOTHING_WINDOW, 11 pixels by default) to suppress leftover speckle in the score itself. Then the app needs a cut-off. A fixed number would be too strict on a quiet scene and too loose on a noisy one, so the app reads two percentiles from that scene's own distribution of D:

  • a strict core threshold, CORE_PERCENTILE (default 99.5);
  • a looser extent threshold, EXTENT_PERCENTILE (default 96.5).

Concretely: sort every D value in this orbit's area of interest and take the value at the 99.5th percentile as DCORE. By construction, only the most extreme 0.5% of pixels in this run clear it. The same scene next month, with different weather and background noise, gets a different number for DCORE but the same meaning: still the top 0.5%. That is what makes the threshold self-calibrating.

3.2Hysteresis: a strict test, a loose test, and connectivity

Hysteresis thresholding is not new to this app. It is the same core idea behind Canny edge detection in ordinary image processing. The general pattern is always: a pixel needs a weak condition to be considered at all, but is only accepted if it is connected to something that clears a strong condition.

It solves one specific problem. A single threshold is always a compromise. Set it strict and you cleanly reject noise, but you also chop the fuzzy, genuine edges off real features. Set it loose and you keep those edges but let a lot of noise through with them. Two thresholds, linked by connectivity, get both at once.

How the linking step works

  1. Build two masks from the same score map: the core mask (D ≥ DCORE, and on steep enough terrain, see 3.3) and the relaxed mask (D ≥ DEXTENT).
  2. Label every group of touching pixels in the relaxed mask. A pixel counts as touching its neighbour even diagonally (8-connectivity).
  3. Any relaxed region that contains at least one core pixel is kept in full, boundary and all. Any relaxed region with none is discarded entirely, however large.

A pixel is never individually promoted or rejected. Whole connected regions are.

Build a mask yourself

This widget runs the second half of the chain on a simulated scene with five real landslides (cyan outlines are the truth) plus a few false-change patches on flat ground. 3.3Terrain awareness: the slope filter

Landslides in this class of terrain do not start on flat ground. So a terrain model (a DEM, here the Copernicus 30 m model) is used to compute the slope of every pixel in degrees. A pixel can only count as a high-confidence core detection if its slope reaches MIN_SOURCE_SLOPE, 8° by default.

This check has nothing to do with the radar data, so it removes a completely different class of false alarm: an unrelated change in backscatter on a flat field, such as flooding, ploughing or harvest. Those change the echo just as strongly, but a flat field cannot slide.

An optional upper limit, MAX_SOURCE_SLOPE, can also exclude near-vertical bare-rock faces where radar geometry creates its own false changes.

A trade-off to know about. A fixed 8° gate is tuned for mountain source areas. In the Jamaica tests, a real slide above Montego Bay sat on only 2 to 3° slopes and was below the gate by design, not by mistake. Lowering the gate for urban or gentle terrain is an option, at the price of more false alarms.

3.4Morphological closing: bridging small gaps

The mask that survives hysteresis is rarely one solid blob. Speckle and small terrain effects can punch pinholes in it, or split what should be one continuous scarp into several almost-touching fragments. Morphological closing is a standard operation from mathematical morphology, the toolbox behind most binary image clean-up. It runs two steps back to back:

  1. Dilation: grow every masked region outward by a fixed number of pixels in every direction.
  2. Erosion: shrink the result back inward by the same amount.

A small gap between two fragments is bridged by the dilation (both sides grow until they touch). The erosion then shrinks the merged shape back, but the bridge, no longer a gap, stays filled. A large empty area far from any masked pixel is never affected, since dilation only grows what is already there. Net effect: small gaps and pinholes disappear while the size and position of real regions barely change.

The size is set by MORPH_CLOSING_KERNEL (default 11 pixels): large enough to bridge realistic gaps, small enough not to weld together two unrelated regions.

3.5Shape filters: size and elongation

After closing, the mask is split into individual connected regions again, and each is checked against two simple physical expectations about what a landslide looks like in a radar image.

MIN_CLUSTER_SIZE_PIXELS · 100

Not too small

A region of only a handful of pixels is far more likely to be a speckle leftover than a slide. Anything below the minimum area is rejected. The flip side: genuinely small slides can be lost (see Limits).

MIN_ELONGATION · 2.0

Not too round

Elongation is the ratio between a region's long axis and its short axis. A landslide scar and its track are typically long and narrow along the slope. A compact, round blob is more likely a patch of changed farmland or noise. Regions below 2:1 are rejected.

3.6Cluster modes: which regions make it into the final mask

What happens to the regions that survive the size and elongation filter is controlled by CLUSTER_MODE. This is a separate decision from thresholding or closing: it is about how much to trust regions that lie far from the strongest detection in the scene. The strongest region(s) act as anchors.

ModeHow it decides what to keepBest suited to
multi (default)Every surviving region whose mean confidence is within MULTI_CLUSTER_RELATIVE_STRENGTH (default 0.6, that is 60%) of the single strongest region becomes its own anchor. Any other region is kept only if it falls inside one of the anchors' proximity zones.A storm that triggered several separate, independent slides in one area: the normal real-world case.
singleExactly one anchor, the single highest-confidence region in the scene. Others are kept only if they touch that anchor's proximity zone.An area known to contain one dominant landslide, or reproducing an older run.
offNo proximity check at all. Every region that passed the size and shape filter is kept as it is.Maximum recall when false alarms are acceptable, or to see what the size and shape filter alone leaves behind.

The proximity zone is a fixed dilation of each anchor's own shape (30 iterations in the implementation). It is large enough that a real secondary lobe of the same landslide, a short distance from the main body, still counts as connected, while an unrelated speckle cluster on the far side of the area does not.

3.7Multi-orbit fusion: two viewpoints are better than one

As Tab 2 explained, radar looks at the ground obliquely. A steep slope facing one satellite track can be squashed or thrown into radar shadow, while the same slope is clearly visible to a track arriving from another direction. Neither is wrong: they are simply looking from different angles.

So the pipeline above is run independently for each track, giving one clean mask per track. Those masks are then combined.

The support-count map

With two or more tracks, the app does not stop at a union and an intersection. It also keeps the arithmetic between them. For every pixel it simply counts how many tracks flagged it:

Support count, per pixelsupport(x,y) = ∑i = tracks 1[ maski(x,y) ]
  • Union (“either”): every pixel with support ≥ 1. More complete, more false alarms.
  • Intersection (“both agree”): every pixel with support equal to the number of tracks. Cleaner, may miss slides only one track can see.
  • Everything in between is a graded confidence. A pixel two of three tracks agree on is not the same as one only a single track saw.

The count is written out as its own output file, so a user can set their own confidence bar afterwards (for example, "trust anything two independent passes agree on") without rerunning the detection.

In a real test (Wayanad, two tracks): requiring both tracks to agree cut the detected area from 6,249 to 2,131 pixels while giving up only 86 of 942 true-positive pixels. Precision against the optical reference rose from 0.15 to 0.40. The Real events tab has the full numbers.

Two apps, one algorithm

How the automatic app triggers the manual app

Everything on the last three tabs (the baseline, the Z-score, the thresholds, the terrain filter, the multi-orbit fusion) lives in exactly one place: the manual app. The automatic app never touches that mathematics. Its entire job is working out which Sentinel-1 images to feed the manual app, and then handing off in a single call.

In this section

4.1The whole chain at a glance

Read the chart from top to bottom. The user supplies two things, an area and an event date. The automatic app turns them into an exact list of satellite tracks with named before and after images. The manual app turns that list into landslide maps.

You provide area of interest (box)You provide event dateOptional terrain model (made automatically if missing)Optional tuning parameters
Automatic applandslide_detection_s1_acd_automatic · finds the data, does no detection maths
  1. Make a terrain modelIf none is supplied, a 30 m DEM is generated for the area.
  2. Search Sentinel-1Query a window around the event date (100 days back, 100 forward by default).
  3. Group by orbitWork out each scene's relative orbit and group the scenes by track.
  4. Filter and rankKeep tracks that cover enough of the area, then rank them.
  5. Select imagesPick the pre-event baseline images and the post-event image(s) for each track.
  6. Import and pre-processFetch missing scenes and run the standard dual-pol pre-processing.

Manual applandslide_detection_s1_acd_manual · all of the detection maths, run once per track
  1. Pre-processCalibrate, fill gaps, despeckle, convert to dB (Tab 2).
  2. BaselinePer-pixel median and spread from the pre-event images (Tab 3).
  3. Z-score and fusionPost-event deviation, drops only, VH and VV combined into D (Tab 3).
  4. Threshold and slopeAdaptive core and extent thresholds, hysteresis, slope gate (Tab 4).

4.2The automatic app, step by step

Its input is just an area and an event date. Its job is to search Sentinel-1, work out the relative orbit of each scene, check footprint coverage, and rank and select orbits and images.

Automatic app

Steps 1 to 3: discover
  1. Auto-generate a DEMIf no terrain model is supplied, one is generated for the area (Copernicus 30 m) with the DEM extractor app. It will be needed for the slope filter.
  2. Search Sentinel-1A search runs over a time window around the event date: DAYS_BACK and DAYS_FORWARD, 100 days each by default. The window must be wide enough to hold several pre-event scenes from the same track.
  3. Group by relative orbitScenes are grouped by satellite track. The relative orbit is not written in the file name, so it is derived from the absolute orbit number (see the box below).

Automatic app

Steps 4 to 6: select and hand off
  1. Filter and rank tracksA track is kept only if its scene footprints cover at least MIN_ORBIT_COVERAGE (10%) of the area. Tracks are then ranked: highest average coverage first, then the smallest gap between the event and the first post-event scene, then the most pre-event images.
  2. Select the imagesFor each track, the best NUMBER_OF_PRE_IMAGES (4 by default) before the event build the baseline, and NUMBER_OF_POST_IMAGES (1 by default) after it are tested against it.
  3. Import, pre-process and delegateAny scene not yet in the workspace is imported and given the same dual-polarization pre-processing the manual app uses. Then everything is passed to the manual app in a single call.

Relative orbit: one number per repeating track

Sentinel-1 circles the Earth roughly 175 times in a 12-day repeat cycle. The same relative orbit number always means the same ground track, so scenes from one relative orbit see a place at the same angle every time. Scene names contain only the absolute orbit number, so the app converts it with an official, mission-specific offset:

Relative orbit from absolute orbit S1A: (abs − 73) mod 175 + 1    S1B: (abs − 27) mod 175 + 1    S1D: (abs − 42) mod 175 + 1

The offset for Sentinel-1C changed on 24 June 2026, so scenes before and after that date use different formulas. Having several scenes per track also allows a pre-event baseline of images taken at 12-day steps.

Why this matters. The statistics assume that the only thing changing between images is the ground. If a pre-event scene came from a different track, the viewing angle would differ and the backscatter would differ for reasons that have nothing to do with a landslide. Grouping by relative orbit is what makes the baseline valid.

4.3The manual app, step by step

Its input is an exact list of tracks, each with named before and after images. It runs the following chain once per track and then combines the tracks. It is exactly the same code path whichever app called it.

Manual app

Steps 1 to 3: build the anomaly score
  1. Pre-processEach GRD image is calibrated and despeckled into dual-pol (VH + VV) linear backscatter through an ESA SNAP workflow, with gaps filled and a 5×5 median filter applied before conversion to dB.
  2. Build the baselinePer-pixel median and standard deviation across every pre-event image, per polarization (floored at SIGMA_FLOOR_DB).
  3. Z-score and dual-pol fusionCombine the post-event image(s) by POST_AGGREGATION, compute the Z-score, keep only backscatter drops, and fuse VH and VV into the single anomaly score D, then smooth it.

Manual app

Steps 4 to 6: turn the score into maps
  1. Threshold and slope gateAdaptive core and extent percentiles, hysteresis linking, and the requirement that core pixels reach MIN_SOURCE_SLOPE.
  2. Clean upMorphological closing, then rejection of regions below MIN_CLUSTER_SIZE_PIXELS or MIN_ELONGATION, and the CLUSTER_MODE proximity rule.
  3. Fuse tracks and write the outputIf several tracks were supplied, combine them (union, intersection and support count), then write GeoTIFF and PNG masks. If a reference raster is given, also score the result.

4.4An example run: what "pre" and "post" really look like

For the Wayanad event (30 July 2024), the automatic app resolved two satellite tracks and delegated the following images to the manual app. Notice the 12-day spacing within each track, four pre-event scenes forming the baseline, and two post-event scenes (this run asked for NUMBER_OF_POST_IMAGES = 2 with POST_AGGREGATION = "median").

The baseline for each track is built only from that track's own pre-event scenes, so viewing geometry is identical. The two tracks are then processed independently and fused at the end. A depth of four pre-event images is the default because it gives a usable median and spread, while more images mean more data to fetch.

4.5What comes out

PropertyValue
File typesGeoTIFF (for analysis) and PNG (for a quick preview)
Pixel values1 landslide · 0 no landslide · 255 no data or insufficient history
Per-track mask{BASENAME}_{TrackLabel}_landslide-mask.tif
Fused masks (two or more tracks){BASENAME}_fused-union_landslide-mask.tif, {BASENAME}_fused-intersection_landslide-mask.tif
Support count{BASENAME}_orbit-support-count.tif: a product in its own right, not just a step
Optional diagnostic plotsbackscatter-change, anomaly-thresholds, overlap-map and, if a reference is given, a confusion-map

Scoring against a reference

If a reference raster of known landslides is supplied (GROUND_TRUTH_FILE), the app scores its result with four standard numbers:

  • Precision: of the pixels flagged, the share that are truly landslide.
  • Recall: of the true landslide pixels, the share that were found.
  • IoU (intersection over union): the overlap divided by the combined area of both masks. It punishes both misses and false alarms.
  • F1: the balance of precision and recall in one number.

4.6Why have both apps?

Reach for the manual app when…

You already know the images

Reprocessing a known event with tuned parameters, comparing specific scenes, or experimenting with the thresholds, without searching the archive again.

Reach for the automatic app when…

A storm just hit and you need whatever evidence exists

The far more common real situation: nobody has pre-selected orbit numbers and file names by hand. Give it an area and a date, and it finds the data and runs the whole chain.

Case studies

Tested on two real disasters

The app was run on landslides that happened in India in 2024 and in Jamaica in 2025, then checked against independent references: a second satellite sensor in the first case, and expert-drawn landslide outlines in the second. The two audits show where the method works well, and where it does not.

0.36IoU of the both-agree map against the optical reference
78%of the optical-mapped corridor also found by radar
2 of 2satellite tracks completed and fused
856 pxpixels where radar and optical agree

AThe event, and the area chosen

Extremely heavy rain, as much as 572 mm in the 48 hours before the event, saturated the slopes above the villages of Mundakkai and Chooralmala in Meppadi panchayat, Kerala. Two slope failures struck in the early hours of 30 July 2024, the second far larger, sending a rockslide-induced debris flow down the Punnapuzha river valley. ISRO's National Remote Sensing Centre measured roughly 86,000 m² of source-zone land movement and a run-out of about 8 km. Officially confirmed deaths exceed 220. It is one of the deadliest single landslide events recorded in India.

The area of interest, about 13 by 13 km (11.457 to 11.576°N, 76.094 to 76.208°E), was centred on Meppadi panchayat so that it contains the affected villages, not drawn around a single press coordinate. Three independently reported landmarks fall well inside it: the landslide headscarp, and the centres of Mundakkai and Chooralmala, with coordinates taken from sources that have nothing to do with the app.

The run

BWhat each track saw

All four panels trace the same corridor from the headscarp, through Mundakkai, toward Chooralmala, not scattered noise on the surrounding terrain. The maps sit on a hillshade of the terrain model. Red marks pixels flagged as landslide.

Point-checked against independently reported landmarks

Beyond pixel statistics, each output was sampled directly at the three landmark coordinates.

LandmarkTrack 63Track 165EitherBoth agreeOptical

Mundakkai is flagged by every radar product, with a support count of 2 at that pixel: both tracks agree independently. The headscarp is caught only by track 165, the same one-track-sees-it asymmetry that multi-orbit fusion exists for. Neither radar nor optical flags the Chooralmala point itself, but both pass close by. A village's nominal centre and the actual debris line are not always the same pixel.

CChecked against a second sensor

No surveyed landslide outline was available for this event. So the radar result was compared with an independent detection of the same event made from Sentinel-2 optical images by another WASDI app, a different sensor and a different algorithm. The optical result was reprojected onto the radar grid and compared pixel by pixel. This is agreement between two independent methods, not validation against surveyed ground truth, but the two share nothing except the real event.

Radar outputDetected pxAgreeing with optical (of 1,094)PrecisionRecallIoU
Track 63 alone3,2858790.2680.8030.251
Track 165 alone5,0959190.1800.8400.174
Either track (union)6,2499420.1510.8610.147
Both agree (intersection)2,1318560.4020.7820.361

Intersection is the clean product

Precision more than doubles

Requiring both tracks to agree cuts detected area from 6,249 to 2,131 pixels while giving up only 86 of 942 agreeing pixels. That is exactly what multi-orbit fusion is designed to do.

Recall is consistently high

78 to 86%

Every radar product, single track, union or intersection, recovers at least 78% of the optical corridor. This is not a marginal or lucky detection.

Radar draws a wider swath

2,131 vs 1,094 pixels

Even the tightest radar map has about twice the optical pixel count. The coarser radar grid (about 20 m) plus the closing step naturally draws a thicker corridor than the fine optical line.

DThe signal itself, not just the mask

This matters because it rules out the main alternative explanation for a strong-looking mask: an unstable score distribution that a threshold happens to slice favourably. Here the signal is visibly real in the raw decibel difference, before any percentile or morphology ever runs. The debris corridor already appears as a coherent drop (blue) in both polarizations.

The score histogram shown in section 3.1 is from this same event: a clean, single-humped distribution with the core threshold sitting naturally in the tail.

EAssessment

Strengths

  • Independent landmarks line up. The headscarp, Mundakkai and the debris corridor all sit where a completely separate run, on a different sensor, also put them.
  • High recall in every fusion mode.
  • Intersection earns its keep. Precision rose from 0.18 to 0.40 against track 165 alone, for a 6 percentage-point recall cost.
  • Both tracks ran cleanly and the signal is real, not a threshold artefact.

Issues

  • A wider swath than the optical map, plausibly the coarser grid plus the closing kernel widening a narrow true corridor.
  • Not ground-truthed. Both compared masks are automated outputs. No surveyed inventory was found for this event.
  • Single-track visibility asymmetry persists: the headscarp is seen by one track only.
  • Village-centre points are a blunt landmark for a narrow debris line.

AThe storm, and how the sites were chosen

Hurricane Melissa formed in the central Caribbean on 22 October 2025 and made landfall near the Westmoreland and St Elizabeth parish border on 28 October as a Category 5 hurricane, the most powerful storm ever recorded striking Jamaica. Sustained winds near 295 km/h and up to 49 inches of rain over the interior mountains triggered widespread flooding and slope failures.

Sites were not picked freehand. Three come from the USGS rapid post-storm imagery assessment, a 5 by 5 km severity grid. Two come from the Copernicus Emergency Management Service (activation EMSR847), whose analysts drew precise landslide footprints by photo-interpretation: human-verified outlines rather than a coarse grid cell. Every area of interest was computed from those datasets, not eyeballed.

BThe five sites, one by one

1. Blue and John Crow Mountains Detected, strong

This 10 by 10 km area sits inside the single highest-severity cell USGS identified anywhere in Jamaica. Both tracks (150 ascending, 40 descending, four pre-event images each) independently found several discrete, elongated clusters on rough terrain, with almost no spatial overlap between them. That is exactly the layover and shadow behaviour that multi-orbit fusion exists to catch, not a flaw.

The score histograms were clean and single-humped on both tracks, with adaptive thresholds sitting well out in the tail (DCORE of 2.49 and 2.92).

4,604pixels flagged (about 2.0% of the area)
1,685 / 2,919track 150 / track 40 pixels
0pixels where the tracks overlap
2. Ginger Hill Detected, one track

Only track 113 produced a result in round 1. Track 150, with images that had worked fine elsewhere, hit a network (SSL certificate) error against the WASDI service mid-run and was skipped by the per-track error handler instead of aborting the run. Replaying the same track locally succeeded, so the best reading is transient network flakiness, not a fault in the detection. The surviving track still delivered a tight, spatially coherent diagonal chain of clusters.

1,776pixels flagged (about 1.5% of the area)
1 of 2tracks contributing
LocalizedUSGS severity of the cell
3. Trout Hall Detected, weak

The weakest of the three USGS-sited detections, appropriately so: it sits in a "localized" cell, not the "major" severity of the Blue Mountains. The core thresholds here (1.88 and 2.84) are markedly lower than at the other rural sites, tracking a genuinely smaller anomaly. The app's relative detection strength across sites 1 to 3 lines up with USGS's own independent severity ranking (4,604, then 1,776, then 841 pixels), a good sign that the anomaly score measures something real and not just noise.

4. Hills above Montego Bay Missed, then partly found

Checked, not assumed. The reference pixels read as valid data that the app simply did not flag, and the georeferencing of detection and reference match to sub-micro-degree precision. It is a real miss, correctly located.

Why, precisely. At the true polygon, track 150's score is real but weak (mean 0.53 against an area background of 0.32). Track 113 barely sees the site at all: only 5 of 454 reference pixels contain valid data, the rest is shadow or layover. The slope there is only 2 to 3°, far below the 8° gate.

5 / 454reference pixels valid on track 113
2 to 3°median slope inside the reference polygon
0pixels detected, round 1

This is the case that moved in round 2 (below).

5. Rennock Lodge, Kingston Missed

The clearest miss of the five. At the reference point, track 150's mean score (0.09) sits below the area's own background mean (0.17): there is no detectable backscatter-change signal there at all, on this track, at any threshold. A second track errored out server-side (the same failure pattern as site 2). Round 2 confirmed the result with a different aggregation mode and every track running, so this is a clean negative and not a partial run.

No tuning would have saved it. It is a small slide on an urban hillside, below what a 20 m radar image can resolve.

CCould tuning have saved the misses?

Rather than guess, the Montego Bay anomaly-score map was cached once (the expensive step) and only thresholding, the slope gate and shape filtering were re-run across 135 parameter combinations, sweeping the two percentiles, the slope gate, the minimum size and the elongation. Every result was checked against the real Copernicus polygon, not just whether the mask was non-empty.

ConfigurationDetected pxTrue-positive px (of 454)RecallIoU
Default: 99.5 / 96.5, slope ≥ 8°, size ≥ 100, elongation ≥ 2.0000.0%0.000
Slope ≥ 4°, size ≥ 203500.0%0.000
Slope ≥ 0°, size ≥ 50639153.3%0.014
Core 99 / extent 95, slope ≥ 4°326173.7%0.022
Best found: core 98 / extent 93, slope ≥ 8°381214.6%0.026

Best-case trade-off

Over 90% false positives

Every configuration that recovers any of the true landslide does so by flooding the rest of the area with unrelated detections. The best IoU was 0.026.

Second track visibility

5 of 454 pixels

Only 1% of the true polygon is valid, non-shadowed data on the second track. Multi-orbit fusion cannot rescue a site that one geometry cannot see.

Slope at the true site

2 to 3°

A physically gentler slope than every rural case: not a misconfigured cut-off.

111 of the 135 combinations did give a non-empty mask, so the parameters can be loosened. But loosening them does not recover the real feature, it only lowers the bar for noise elsewhere. For these two sites the limit is the physical signal, not the thresholds that sit on top of it.

DRound 2: does combining more post-event images help?

Landslide scars do not vanish the day after the storm, so a natural follow-up is to give the app more post-event passes to choose from, combined differently. All five sites were re-run with 4 post-event images (up from 1) and a search window of 100 days forward (up from 60). The aggregation was split by hypothesis: median on the three rural hits (to suppress false positives) and max_anomaly on the two urban misses (to catch a fading signal).

An operational cost we did not expect. Raising the images per track from 5 to 8 visibly raised the failure rate of individual tracks: 4 of the 5 first-attempt runs lost at least one track, and Montego Bay lost both. Every failed track ran successfully when replayed locally with identical inputs, and explicit certificate errors turned up in several logs, pointing to transient connectivity problems made more likely by more sequential per-image network calls. The cases needed retries before both tracks completed together.

Montego Bay: a real, partial recovery

With max_anomaly and 4 post-event images, track 150 went from 0 detected pixels to 344, of which 25 land on the actual Copernicus polygon. More telling than the numbers: the detected region is one large, coherent, elongated shape sitting at the downslope end of the true landslide and touching it, not scattered noise. The cost is visible too: the score distribution shifted much higher (the core threshold rose from about 2.1 to 6.16), the expected price of taking a per-pixel maximum over more images.

0 → 25true-positive pixels
0.000 → 0.032IoU
2.1 → 6.16core threshold

Kingston: confirmed, still nothing

Zero detected pixels again, but this time all three tracks completed, so it is a clean negative. It rules out "a single-image fluke" and reinforces that there is no usable backscatter drop at this site on any date checked, under any aggregation mode.

The hits, re-tested with median

Siteclosest (round 1)median (round 2)ChangeIoU vs round 1Cross-track agreement
Blue Mountains4,604 px4,308 px−6%0.3360 px (both rounds)
Ginger Hill1,776 px (1 track only)2,348 px (2 tracks fused)first full fusion-161 px, first time ever
Trout Hall841 px645 px−23%0.2500 px (both rounds)

Bottom line. max_anomaly delivered a real, if small, recovery at Montego Bay with a plausible shape: worth adopting for weak or fading signals despite its higher false-positive exposure. median never degraded a detection into noise, but its false-positive benefit remains unproven because the coarse USGS grid cannot grade a boundary-level change. And the clearest outcome of the whole round was not about aggregation at all: getting both tracks to succeed together at Ginger Hill produced the one thing no single-track run can, independent cross-track confirmation (161 pixels).

EWhat the Jamaica tests teach

What worked

  • Detection strength tracked independent severity (major, then localized), without the app ever seeing that ranking.
  • Multi-orbit fusion earned its keep: at the Blue Mountains the two tracks found almost entirely different clusters on the same slope.
  • Self-calibrating thresholds held up: every successful run had a clean single-humped score histogram, no per-scene tuning needed.
  • Failures degraded gracefully: a single track erroring out did not sink the run.
  • Honest misses: where it missed, it missed cleanly, with no false detections invented to compensate.

What did not

  • Blind to small, gentle, urban slides: 2 of 2 misses against precise ground truth, against 3 of 3 hits on rural mountain terrain.
  • The terrain gate assumes rural-steep source areas. A fixed 8° gate excludes real slides on gentler hillsides by design.
  • No feedback when a track is structurally blind: a "successful" track can see only 1% of a site, and nothing in the output says so.
  • Per-track failures are silent at run level.
  • Parameters cannot rescue a weak physical signal: 135 combinations, best IoU 0.026.
Honest limits

What to keep in mind, and where it is heading

The app produces a map of candidate landslides quickly, over a large area, whatever the weather. Treat it as a way to point people, drones and optical imagery at the right slopes, not as a final damage count. This page collects what the validation work showed about where it is strong and where it is not.

In this section

6.1Where it is strong

Terrain

Steep, rural, mountainous source areas

All three rural sites in Jamaica and the whole Wayanad corridor were detected. This is the terrain the slope gate and shape filters were designed for.

Agreement

Independent checks line up

Radar matched an independent optical detection with 78 to 86% recall at Wayanad, and its relative strength followed an independent expert severity ranking in Jamaica.

Robustness

Self-calibrating and honest

Percentile thresholds adapt to each scene. Where the app misses, it misses cleanly, without inventing detections.

6.2Known limits

  • Small slides can hide. A slide smaller than a few radar pixels (a pixel is about 20 m) may not change the echo enough, and the minimum size filter removes tiny regions by design.
  • Gentle and urban slopes. The steepness filter is set for mountain source areas. A real slide on a 2 to 3° urban hillside was below the gate. Lowering the gate recovers little without flooding the map with false alarms.
  • Shadow and layover. Some slopes cannot be seen from some tracks. In one test a second track saw only about 1% of the true slide area.
  • Other changes look similar. Flooded fields, ploughing or harvest can change the echo. The terrain and shape checks remove many, not all.
  • Needs earlier images. The baseline needs several pre-event scenes from the same track. Where the archive is thin, the area is marked "insufficient history".
  • Not a survey. Results should be confirmed on the ground or with other imagery. At Wayanad both compared maps were automatic outputs, and the radar swath is wider than the optical line.

6.3Reading an empty map

A map with no detections is not the same as "no landslide". There are at least three different reasons a pixel can be empty, and the output does not yet tell them apart:

  1. nothing happened there;
  2. something happened but it was too small, too gentle or too weak to register;
  3. the satellite track could not see that ground at all (shadow, layover or no data).

Rule of thumb. Treat a detection as strong evidence and an empty area as unknown when the slopes are gentle, built-up, small in scale, or seen by only one track. That is why the roadmap below includes observability masks and confidence flags.

6.4Where it is heading

Susceptibility maps

Use known landslide hazard as a soft hint

The World Bank / GFDRR global landslide hazard layer can act as a soft prior to cut false positives. Users could also bring their own susceptibility map.

Drone confirmation

Drone images as ground truth

Drone surveys of a few slopes can confirm detections and tune thresholds for a region.

Radar exclusion maps

Say where radar cannot see

Masks for shadow, layover and no-data areas, and a report of the share of each track's eligible area actually observed, so a blank result is not mistaken for "no landslide".

Radar plus optical

Combine with the Sentinel-2 app

Joint detection that uses optical imagery when the sky is clear and radar when it is not.

Ideas from the validation work

  1. Surface track-level observability. Report what fraction of each track's eligible area was valid data, so a "successful" track that was blind at a site does not read as a clean negative.
  2. Make the terrain gate context-aware. Offer a lower or user-set minimum slope profile for urban and peri-urban areas.
  3. Escalate per-track failures. Flag a silently dropped track at run level, so users decide whether to rerun.
  4. Treat "zero detections" as its own outcome, with a confidence flag tied to valid-pixel coverage and slope-gate exclusion area.
  5. Use precise reference data where it exists. Wire emergency-mapping outlines to the scoring option automatically after an event.
Get started

Run it on your own area

The app runs in the WASDI cloud, so there is nothing to install. All you need is a WASDI account, an area and an event date. Everything else has a sensible default, which this page lists in full so that you can tune it when you need to.

In this section

7.1Quick start

  1. Open WASDI and create a workspace. Your results are saved there.
  2. Find the Landslide Detection (Sentinel-1) app in the WASDI marketplace and open it.
  3. Draw a box around the area of interest. Start with something around 10 by 10 km.
  4. Enter the event date. The app looks for radar images before it and after it.
  5. Run the app. It picks the images and satellite tracks, runs the detection, and writes the maps to your workspace.

What you get back

  • A landslide mask for each satellite track.
  • A combined mask for "either track" and one for "both agree".
  • An orbit support count showing how many tracks flagged each pixel.
  • Optional diagnostic plots that show the radar change and the thresholds used.

Tip. Use both agree when you need few false alarms, and either track when missing a slide would be worse than checking an extra one. The support count lets you choose in between.

If you see…Try…At the price of…
Too many false alarmsRaise CORE_PERCENTILE, use the "both agree" mask, raise MIN_SOURCE_SLOPE or the size and elongation limits.Missing weaker or smaller slides.
Slides that are missing or clippedLower CORE_PERCENTILE or EXTENT_PERCENTILE, use the "either" mask, lower MIN_CLUSTER_SIZE_PIXELS.More false alarms.
A signal that fades quicklyUse several post-event images with max_anomaly.More exposure to one-off noisy dips; a higher score distribution overall.
Very noisy resultsUse several post-event images with median, or a larger SCORE_SMOOTHING_WINDOW.Blurring a signal that partly recovers.
Gentle or urban terrainLower MIN_SOURCE_SLOPE.Flat-ground false alarms such as flooding.
Fragmented detectionsRaise MORPH_CLOSING_KERNEL.Welding together unrelated regions.
One dominant slide expectedSet CLUSTER_MODE to single.Losing independent slides far from the anchor.

7.5Sources

  • Wayanad event details and coordinates: The Landslide Blog (AGU Eos), "The 30 July 2024 Wayanad landslides in Kerala, India"; 2024 Wayanad landslides; village coordinates from Mundakkai and Chooralmala.
  • Independent radar-based damage assessment of the same event: Data for Public Good, Landslide Damage Assessment, Wayanad, Kerala (not spatially compared here).
  • Jamaica: USGS, 2025 Hurricane Melissa Landslide Hazards and its rapid imagery assessment data release (DOI 10.5066/P1JMKWMF); Copernicus Emergency Management Service, activation EMSR847; NOAA National Hurricane Center report AL132025.
  • Radar background: NASA ARSET, Using SAR for Landslide Detection; ESA SNAP tutorials, Sentinel-1 SAR pre-processing; WASDI Python tutorial.
  • Radar data: Copernicus Sentinel-1. Terrain: Copernicus 30 m DEM. Case-study figures were produced from WASDI runs of the landslide detection apps in September 2026.
